sharedText: this is the thing which I have
reason: A six-word run and a genuine formal parallel — both sentences are a revealer telling a hearer that what follows is the disclosed thing — and still not a link. Joseph's 'This is the thing which I have spoken unto Pharaoh' and Alma's 'this is the thing of which I do know' diverge at the verb, which is where all the meaning is: Joseph has spoken a dream's interpretation, Alma has inquired and been told. The frame 'this is the thing which' is KJV disclosure boilerplate (Exodus 16:16, 16:32, 35:4, Leviticus 8:5, 9:6, Numbers 30:1), and nothing in Genesis 41 bears on souls, death, or the interval Alma is describing.

sharedText: they shall rise from the dead
reason: The stream's top candidate for both 40:5 and 40:9, on a six-word run, and it is the wrong chapter of the right subject. Mark 12:18-27 is the Sadducees' riddle about the woman with seven husbands, and Jesus' answer is about marriage, not about an interval between death and resurrection; nothing else in the verse or its context surfaces in Alma 40. 'Rise from the dead' is distributed across some twenty KJV verses. Where Alma 40 does touch the Sadducees it is at 40:2, and the phrase there is 'there is no resurrection', which the register sends to 1 Corinthians 15:12 with the Sadducee verses named.

Four shared words in the same order and an opposed sense. Deuteronomy's 'no part nor inheritance' is a statement about the priestly tribe's landlessness and it is a privilege, not a punishment — Levi has no allotment because the LORD is his inheritance. Five KJV verses say it (Deuteronomy 10:9, 12:12, 14:27, 14:29, 18:1) and all five are that same provision. Alma 40:13 is denying the wicked dead a share in the Spirit as the consequence of their own choice. The only KJV verse in which the frame denies a man a part in the Spirit is Acts 8:21, to Simon Magus, and that is filed as a link at this verse at low confidence with its own whyNot.

sharedText: led captive by the will of the Devil
reason: The verse's closing clause is the fourth appearance in Alma of the snare-and-captivity sentence of 2 Timothy 2:26 ('who are taken captive by him at his will', a KJV singleton). It is adjudicated at Alma 12:6, with 12:11 and 12:17 recorded there as recurrences; 40:13 is a fifth instance of the same speaker's settled formula rather than a fresh borrowing, and it adds nothing the earlier verses do not have. Registered here because a reader meeting 'led captive by the will of the Devil' at the climax of Alma 40 will want to be told where the argument for it is made.

The devils of Gadara begging to enter the swine is the machine's proposal for 'the spirit of the Devil did enter into them', and it is a real thematic neighbour — the KJV's other scene of spirits entering a body at their own request. But the four shared words are ordinary, Luke 8 supplies no 'house' and no 'possession', and what Alma 40:13 actually reproduces is the figure of the possessed person as a house, which belongs to Matthew 12:43-45 and Luke 11:24-26. The link is filed there.

'Both soul and body' occurs in exactly two KJV verses and this is one of them, so the rarity is real; the sense is not. Isaiah 10:18 is the burning of Assyria's forest and fruitful field, where 'both soul and body' is a totalizing idiom for utter consumption and the standard-bearer faints. Alma 40:21 has soul and body reunited and standing before God. The other KJV occurrence, Matthew 10:28, is nearer the subject — God able to destroy both soul and body in hell — but its sense is destruction where Alma's is restoration, and the phrase is doing no work in Alma beyond naming the two halves he has spent the chapter separating. The link at this verse is Revelation 20:12-13.

A five-word run and the machine's best candidate for the chapter's last verse, matching a regulation about ovens and pot-ranges defiled by a carcase falling on them, which are to be broken down. The Book of Mormon's 'they are unclean' is a verdict on persons at the judgment. The one genuine point of contact is that Alma's uncleanness is cultic rather than moral vocabulary, which is a Levitical inheritance in general and not a borrowing from this verse.

sharedText: no unclean thing can inherit the Kingdom of God
reason: The sentence is adjudicated at Alma 11:37, where Amulek offers it as a divine quotation and the note shows it has two KJV parents and no KJV existence — Ephesians 5:5's 'no whoremonger, nor unclean person' having 'any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God', and 1 Corinthians 6:9-10's list who 'shall not inherit the kingdom of God'. Alma 40:26 is the same formula in the same book, with one change worth recording here: Amulek said 'Kingdom of Heaven', a phrase confined in the KJV to Matthew, and Alma says 'Kingdom of God', which is the form 1 Corinthians 6:9-10 and Galatians 5:21 actually use. The formula has drifted toward its Pauline source rather than away from it.
